bar: Research cycle-138 criteria U1-U6, front-door only, all six to pass: U1 FOR (verb+object job stated) · U2 GET (a named, countable deliverable) · U3 FIRST ACTION + EFFORT (step 1 + minutes + what-you'll-need up front) · U4 LEVEL + PREREQUISITE (one-clause honest gate) · U5 PROOF (a worked example visible at the front door) · U6 NO UNPAID JARGON (terms glossed at first use).

skills.title: Set up the asset registry
skills.gets_you: You will have one named list of every character, place and prop in your film, locked before you generate anything — so shot 40 still matches shot 1.

skills.title: Build the per-scene shotlist
skills.gets_you: You will have a written plan for every shot in a scene — its exact prompt, length and look — that you generate from instead of re-inventing shots in the chat window.

skills.title: Stress-test a scene before generating
skills.gets_you: You will know whether a scene actually works — who wants what, what blocks them, what flips — before spending a single credit generating it.

skills.title: Draw the blocking diagram
skills.gets_you: You will have a simple colour-coded map of where every character stands in a complicated shot, so multi-person scenes stop coming out scrambled.

skills.title: Add depth maps for room-heavy scenes
skills.gets_you: Your rooms will stay the same room: furniture, doors and windows hold their places across every shot in the location.

skills.title: Write island prompts
skills.gets_you: Every prompt you write will work on its own — the model has no memory of your last shot, and after this, it will not need any.

skills.title: Lock the Voice Bible
skills.gets_you: Your character will sound like the same person in every scene, because the exact same voice instructions go into every generation, word for word.

skills.title: Chain scenes with video references
skills.gets_you: Each new scene will start from your last finished scene's actual video, so the film flows as one piece instead of drifting apart shot by shot.

skills.title: Work out what a long film really costs
skills.gets_you: You will know the honest price range of your long film before you start — including re-generations — so the budget does not die halfway through production.

skills.title: Run the five post stages
skills.gets_you: You will have a finishing order for a long film — assembly, rough cut, supervision, fine cut, lock — so 'nearly done' stops lasting forever.

skills.title: Audit long-form failure modes
skills.gets_you: You will catch the nine ways long AI films usually fall apart while yours can still be fixed cheaply.

skills.title: Staff a small AI feature crew
skills.gets_you: If your production grows, you will know which jobs exist, what each one owns, and who to give them to — so nothing important is nobody's job.

skills.title: Run an async remote production
skills.gets_you: Reference for later: how a small team in different time zones makes one film together — one shared project, jobs split by craft, no drift between collaborators.

skills.title: Run a five-day sprint
skills.gets_you: Reference for later: how fluent directors turn out a trailer-grade piece in five days — a method to grow into once the basics are fast.

skills.title: Build a hybrid pipeline
skills.gets_you: You will have a plan where the emotional moments are filmed for real and AI builds the impossible parts around them — feelings that land, spectacle that still happens.

skills.title: Commit to an authored style
skills.gets_you: You will have picked a look that hides AI's small mistakes instead of exposing them — the single cheapest quality upgrade a first film can make.

skills.title: Direct a photoreal character piece
skills.gets_you: You will have a realistic short that feels acted rather than generated: a real script, one point of view, faces carrying the story.

skills.title: Apply long-form discipline to shorts
skills.gets_you: Your short film will hold together like a long one: every shot mapped, identities locked, drafts cheap — no character or room changing between shots.

skills.title: Run the entry-killer audit

skills.title: Check competition delivery compliance
skills.gets_you: You will know your entry actually follows the competition's rules — format, length, disclosure — before you submit, not after a disqualification email.

skills.title: Plan a competition entry
skills.gets_you: You will have a production plan built backwards from the competition's deadline and constraints, so the film gets finished, not just started.

skills.title: Assemble the delivery package
skills.gets_you: You will hand over everything a competition asks for — the film file, the watermark, the packshot, the public post — assembled in one go.

skills.title: Budget credits for a competition entry
skills.gets_you: You will know how many credits a competition entry really takes, so a 3–5 minute film does not run out of money at minute two.

skills.title: Lock the style bible
skills.gets_you: You will have the one sentence that describes your film's look, ready to paste into every prompt — the habit that makes a film look like one film.

skills.title: Write the Identity Block
skills.gets_you: You will be able to describe a character once, in a reusable block, so they look identical every time they appear.

skills.title: Write the Motion Block
skills.gets_you: You will be able to say exactly what happens in a shot — one action, one camera move — in the form models follow most reliably.

skills.title: Run the 720p draft loop
skills.gets_you: You will test every shot cheaply first and only pay full price for the takes that already work — most of your budget stays unspent.

skills.title: Decide what to upscale
skills.gets_you: You will know which finished shots deserve expensive high-resolution renders and which never do — and stop paying to upscale rejects.

skills.title: Cut sound-first
skills.gets_you: You will have a version of your film that already works with your eyes closed — dialogue and sound cut first, picture fitted to it.

skills.title: Structure a trailer cut
skills.gets_you: You will have a 60–90 second trailer shape — hook, escalation, title — that makes a short film feel like an event.

skills.title: Debug a failing prompt
skills.gets_you: When a generation ignores you, you will have a method — change one thing at a time — that finds the fix instead of burning credits on random re-rolls.

skills.title: Choose a model for dialogue + lip sync
skills.gets_you: You will know which model to pay for when characters talk on screen, so lips and voices match instead of floating apart.

skills.title: Choose a model for fast action
skills.gets_you: You will know which model keeps chases and fights readable and fast, instead of melting them into blur.

skills.title: Choose the cheapest draft model
skills.gets_you: You will know the cheapest model that still answers 'does this shot work?', so testing ideas costs pennies.

skills.title: Choose a model for product commercials
skills.gets_you: You will know which model makes a product look expensive on camera — macro detail, clean orbits, a packshot that sells.

skills.title: Choose a model for anime production
skills.gets_you: You will know which models actually speak anime — cel shading and impact frames — instead of imitating it badly.

skills.title: Choose a model for photoreal faces
skills.gets_you: You will know which model to trust with faces in close-up, where every flaw is visible.

skills.title: Choose a model for long takes
skills.gets_you: You will know which model can hold one long shot together without you stitching fragments in the edit.

skills.title: Choose a model for talking heads
skills.gets_you: You will know which model gives a clean, believable person-talking-to-camera shot for interviews and explainers.

skills.title: Choose a model for stylized 3D
skills.gets_you: You will know which model delivers that polished animated-feature look for stylised 3D characters.

skills.title: Choose a model for music videos
skills.gets_you: You will know which model cuts to a beat without falling apart — style, speed and rhythm in one pick.

skills.title: Fix morphing faces
skills.gets_you: A face that keeps melting or changing mid-shot will hold still and stay the same person.

skills.title: Fix identity drift across scenes

skills.title: Fix bad lip sync
skills.gets_you: Dialogue that looked dubbed will line up with the voice, by routing it through the sync path that fits the scene.

skills.title: Fix the plasticky AI look

skills.title: Fix flicker and boiling
skills.gets_you: Textures that crawl and shimmer between frames will settle down so the shot stops looking haunted.

skills.title: Fix muddy AI audio
skills.gets_you: Dull, washy AI audio will come out clear enough that dialogue is understood the first time.

skills.title: Budget a 3-minute short
skills.gets_you: You will know what a good 3-minute short really costs, in credits and dollars, before you generate the first shot.

skills.title: Budget a 20-minute film
skills.gets_you: You will know what a 20-minute film really costs — retakes included — while there is still time to change the plan.

skills.title: Budget a 90-minute feature
skills.gets_you: You will know what a feature-length AI film really costs, and where that money actually goes.

skills.title: Deliver for competitions
skills.gets_you: You will have a finished film file that meets competition specs exactly — right format, watermark, packshot — ready to upload.

skills.title: Deliver for social (9:16)
skills.gets_you: Your film will work as a vertical phone video without the important parts being cropped off the sides.

skills.title: Deliver a trailer master
skills.gets_you: You will have a finished 60–90 second trailer file, mastered and ready to post or submit.

skills.title: Direct an AI voiceover
skills.gets_you: Your AI narrator or character will sound directed — paced, emphasised, human — instead of reading like a satnav.

skills.title: Build the SFX bed
skills.gets_you: Your scenes will sound like places: a layered bed of background, effects and Foley under every shot, instead of silence between lines.

skills.title: Brief AI music (Suno-style)
skills.gets_you: You will be able to ask an AI music tool for a score cue and actually get back something your film can use.

skills.title: Choose the lip-sync route
skills.gets_you: For every dialogue scene, you will know which lip-sync method to use — the one that fits the words, the budget and the deadline.

skills.title: Run the final mix pass
skills.gets_you: Your finished film will sound balanced on a phone, a laptop and a TV — dialogue first, nothing buried, nothing blaring.

skills.title: Shoot a dialogue scene
skills.gets_you: You will have filmed a complete two-person conversation that cuts together like a real scene — both sides, reactions, rhythm.

skills.title: Shoot a chase sequence
skills.gets_you: You will have a chase the audience can actually follow — fast, exciting, and never confusing about who is where.

skills.title: Shoot a product spot
skills.gets_you: You will have a 30-second product film — macro beauty shot, orbit, lifestyle moment — that looks like it cost an agency.

skills.title: Shoot a horror short
skills.gets_you: You will have a horror short that scares by what it withholds — dread built from sound, shadow and timing, not jump-scare spam.

skills.title: Shoot a music video
skills.gets_you: You will have a music video whose pictures hit the beat and change with the song's energy.

skills.title: Cut a trailer
skills.gets_you: You will have cut your footage into a 60–90 second trailer with a hook, a build and a title moment.

skills.title: Shoot an interview
skills.gets_you: You will have an interview that looks and sounds credible — the talking-head backbone of documentaries and explainers.

skills.title: Shoot a dream sequence
skills.gets_you: You will have a dream sequence that feels dreamlike yet emotionally clear — strange images, unbroken feeling.

skills.title: Shoot a fight scene
skills.gets_you: You will have a fight that reads: the audience sees every hit, knows the geography, and feels the impact.

skills.title: Cut a montage
skills.gets_you: You will have compressed weeks or years into a sequence that still moves the audience in one direction.

skills.title: Shoot an establishing sequence
skills.gets_you: You will be able to tell an audience where they are, when it is, and how to feel — in under 15 seconds.

skills.title: Land the finale button
skills.gets_you: Your film will end on the image people remember and describe to friends afterwards.

skills.title: Direct anime (sakuga)
skills.gets_you: Your action scenes will look like real anime — painted backgrounds, impact frames, movement with snap and weight.

skills.title: Direct Ghibli-style pastoral
skills.gets_you: Your scenes will have that hand-painted, gentle, drifting-cloud calm — landscapes the audience wants to live inside.

skills.title: Direct Pixar-style 3D
skills.gets_you: Your characters will have the appeal and clarity of a big-studio animated feature — expressions that read instantly.

skills.title: Direct western 2D cartoon
skills.gets_you: Your cartoon will have flat colour, thick outlines and snappy limited animation — the classic TV-cartoon energy.

skills.title: Direct claymation
skills.gets_you: Your film will feel handmade — fingerprints, stepped motion, real-clay charm — instead of computer-smooth.

skills.title: Direct photoreal drama
skills.gets_you: Your drama will look like it was filmed with real actors — intimate, quiet, and believable enough that nobody asks how.

skills.title: Direct photoreal action
skills.gets_you: Your action will look like a theatrical trailer — kinetic, glossy, and physically convincing.

skills.title: Direct living oil painting
skills.gets_you: Your film will move like a living oil painting — dense brushstrokes in motion, a look no live camera can get.

skills.title: Kill the AI look
skills.gets_you: Your footage will stop looking generated: grain, lens character and restraint added in the right order, so audiences see a film, not a demo.

skills.title: Cut with J/L cuts
skills.gets_you: Your cuts will flow: dialogue starting before the picture changes (and lingering after) hides edits and makes AI footage feel continuous.

skills.title: Separate identity from motion
skills.gets_you: Your characters will stop changing appearance between shots, because who they are and what they do are written separately in every prompt.

skills.title: Build first/last-frame transitions
skills.gets_you: You will be able to morph smoothly between two composed images — a transition that looks designed, not accidental.

skills.title: Chain with relay frames
skills.gets_you: Long sequences will hold together: every clip starts on the previous clip's last frame, so the film never visibly restarts.

skills.title: Re-anchor references
skills.gets_you: Before a character's face drifts too far, you will have refreshed their reference — drift fixed while it is still invisible to audiences.

skills.title: Bake the look into plates
skills.gets_you: Your look will survive every generation, because the grade and lens character live in the starting image itself, not in words the model can ignore.

skills.title: Stage with blocking diagrams
skills.gets_you: Complicated multi-character shots will come out staged the way you drew them, not scrambled.

skills.title: Maintain the Voice Bible
skills.gets_you: Your character's voice direction will be identical in every generation — the same written direction, pasted verbatim, every time.

skills.title: Draft at 720p, upscale winners
skills.gets_you: You will prove every shot at cheap resolution first and only pay full price for winners — the discipline that saves most of a budget.

skills.title: Build character sheet composites
skills.gets_you: You will have a reference sheet of your character from several angles that keeps them the same person in every shot.

skills.title: Lock the style bible
skills.gets_you: Every shot in your film will share one look, because one written style sentence — locked on day one — goes into every prompt word for word.

skills.title: Enforce one motion per prompt
skills.gets_you: Your shots will do one thing cleanly instead of three things badly — the single habit that fixes more prompts than any other.

skills.title: Use face-erased sheets for new angles
skills.gets_you: You will get your character from new camera angles without their face changing, by starting from sheets with the face left blank.

skills.title: Prefer video references over text
skills.gets_you: Your scenes will continue from what is actually on screen — showing the model the previous video instead of describing it and hoping.

skills.title: Apply the negatives policy
skills.gets_you: Your prompts will get what you ask for more often, because they say what TO show instead of listing what to avoid (which models often render anyway).

skills.title: Direct gaze and eyelines
skills.gets_you: Your characters will look at the right things — eyelines that match across cuts, so conversations feel like they happen in one room.

skills.title: Lay the ambience bed
skills.gets_you: Your film will sound like one continuous place, because one unbroken background sound runs under all of it.

skills.title: Prefer long takes over cut-stitching
skills.gets_you: Your scenes will flow in long unbroken shots instead of stitched fragments — solved while generating, not faked in the edit.

skills.title: Screen for cold viewers
skills.gets_you: You will find the confusing, boring and broken moments you have gone blind to — by testing the cut on fresh viewers before it ships.

skills.title: Rewrite emotions as tactics
skills.gets_you: Your characters will act believably, because you will direct them with things they can DO ('she hides the letter') instead of feelings models cannot render ('she is sad').

skills.title: Write the director's read
skills.gets_you: Before generating a scene, you will have written what it is really about and how each character shows it physically — the note that makes performances agree with each other.

skills.title: Ration close-ups
skills.gets_you: Your close-ups will land like punches, because they are saved for the emotional peaks instead of spent everywhere.

skills.title: Decide AI vs hybrid performance
skills.gets_you: You will know when a scene needs a real human performer at its centre — and when AI can honestly carry it.

skills.title: Unify before grading
skills.gets_you: All your shots will match each other — same light, same colour world — before any creative look is applied, so the film stops looking stitched from different cameras.

skills.title: Run the de-plasticize stack
skills.gets_you: The waxy, over-smooth AI skin and candy colour will be gone — desaturate, grain, soften, in the order that works.

skills.title: Grade with scopes, not eyes
skills.gets_you: Your colours will be right on every screen, not just yours — measured with the waveform and vectorscope tools the pros use.

skills.title: Run the restraint pass
skills.gets_you: Your characters will stop over-acting: smaller, quieter, more believable performances, directed with restraint instead of melodrama.

skills.title: Choose the dialogue road
skills.gets_you: For every dialogue scene you will pick the right route — the model speaks it natively, or you record the voice and sync it — before it costs you re-renders.

skills.title: Direct TTS voices through text
skills.gets_you: Your text-to-speech voices will sound directed, because you will write the punctuation, pauses and emphasis that are the only controls these tools give you.

skills.title: Run the dead-eyes checklist
skills.gets_you: You will be able to spot lifeless AI eyes in seconds — and fix them by giving the eyes something to do.

skills.title: Lock the scene after approval

skills.title: Choose the release path
skills.gets_you: You will choose where your film actually gets seen — AI-native distributor, YouTube, festivals, or your own site — with the trade-offs in plain view.

skills.title: Release on YouTube safely

skills.title: Run the disclosure pass

skills.title: Verify likeness clearance

skills.title: Clear AI music rights properly

skills.title: Run the cue sheet

skills.title: Run the grade sheet
skills.gets_you: You will have a working grade sheet (the Grade Sheet page) that matches every scene to its reference look and tells you when the colour is locked.

skills.title: Run the cut sheet
skills.gets_you: You will have a working cut sheet (the Cut Sheet page) that inspects every shot in your edit and tells you when the picture is ready to lock.

skills.title: Run the take sheet
skills.gets_you: You will have a working take sheet (the Take Sheet page) that logs every performance beat and tells you when the acting is ready to lock.

skills.title: Run the longform sheet
skills.gets_you: You will have a working longform sheet (the Longform Sheet page) that tracks every scene of a long production and tells you when the film is ready to lock.
